A pear-shaped four-string tenor lute appeared in 1924, and from 1927 there were models with a wooden soundbox. It rose in the 1930s as jazz bands and dance orchestras took up the six-string guitar, and it was valued again in the Dixieland revival and the folk boom. Electric models exist from the late 1930s, solid bodies from the 1950s, and there was a revival in the early twenty-first century.

The tenor guitar is a four-string guitar, a slightly smaller variant of the steel-string acoustic or the electric guitar, with a mixed sounding classification, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.322-4, found mainly in the United States. The body is usually guitar-shaped and may be a flat-top or archtop wooden body, a metal resonator or a solid body; the scale length is about 21 to 23 inches, and it is commonly tuned in fifths C3−G3−D4−A4. It can accompany or play lead. It was first made for four-string tenor banjo players doubling on guitar in jazz bands and dance orchestras; it later appeared in country, the Dixieland revival, folk, bebop, rhythm and blues and nu metal.
